q: Which method of compensation under the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP) ts typically applied when an architect maintains a continuing relationship with a client involving a series of projects, and is paid a fixed professional fee in addition to reimbursement for technical time and overhead expenses?
n: Professional fee plus expenses suits a continuing relationship over a series of projects: a fixed fee plus reimbursement of technical time and overhead. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines (methods of compensation).

q: Which method of compensation under the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP) is particularly suited for government projects due to their extensive paperwork and time-consuming procedural requirements, and involves a predetermined amount agreed upon regardless of actual construction cost?
n: A lump sum or fixed fee, a set amount agreed regardless of construction cost, is suited to government projects with heavy paperwork. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines (methods of compensation).

q: A method of compensation based on a reasonable profit on specific revenues of a project engagement or based on a measure of value to the client.
n: Value pricing bases the fee on a reasonable profit on specific revenues of the engagement or on a measure of value to the client, such as 4–6% of gross rental for building administration. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205, Secs. 10.2.1 and 10.3.

q: The architect engaged as a Building Administrator and/or Property Manager can be compensated based on value pricing by how many percent based on gross rental?
n: An architect engaged as Building Administrator and/or Property Manager and paid by value pricing receives 4% to 6% of gross rental. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205, Sec. 10.3.

q: Minimum and maximum post-construction RPF
n: The RPF for post-construction services under value pricing is 4% to 6% of gross rental (gross income). Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205, Sec. 10.3.

q: According to the Methods of Compensation under the SPP, what is the range of the Recommended Professional Fee (RPF) for post-construction services rendered on an income-generating commercial building, when the fee is computed using a value-based pricing model tied to gross rental income?
n: Value-based pricing for post-construction services is 4% to 6% of gross rental. This incentive-type fee rewards efficient, economical operation. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines (PRBOA Res. No. 06, s. 2016), SPP Doc. 205, Sec. 10.3.

q: From among the choices, which is the ideal method of compensation for Professional Consulting Services?
n: For consulting engagements made of intermittent personal services, the SPP names Per Diem or Hourly Basis as particularly suited, compensating the consultant for all time devoted to the work, including travel time. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 209, Sec. 4.3.12.1.

q: Most appropriate method of compensation for site planning services
n: Site planning for building sites is paid by area: the RPF is a unit rate per square meter (₱5.00/m², or ₱50,000 per hectare, for the first 5 hectares). This is the Unit Cost method. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 203, Sec. 7.3.2.1.

q: Which method of compensation is most appropriate for an architect performing non-creative work?
n: MDPE is a cost-based method that applies only to non-creative work such as research, data gathering and report preparation. It counts technical hours spent, which cannot measure the value of creative design. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, Sec. 4.3.8.1.

q: Most common method of compensation
n: Percentage of Project Construction Cost is the method most commonly used for regular design services. It is the first method listed in SPP Doc. 202, and the RPF tables are stated as a percentage of PCC. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202, Sec. 6.2.1.

q: An architectural firm is monitoring the performance of several ongoing projects. One project has generated significant client appreciation and has already been billed according to the agreed professional fee. However, management wants to determine whether the project is financially healthy from the firm's perspective. Which indicator would provide the MOST reliable measure?
o: The professional fee has been invoiced and collected according to the service agreement.
The project maintains a positive relationship between the architect, contractor, and owner throughout construction.
The client expresses satisfaction and is likely to commission repeat projects.
The actual hours expended compared with the budgeted hours allocated to the project.
n: Being invoiced, having a happy client or good relationships does not show whether the project made money. Comparing actual hours expended against the budgeted man-hours shows whether the fee is covering the firm's direct personnel cost. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, Sec. 4.3.8 (fees built from technical hours × rate).

q: The rate of the architect, the consultants, technical staff, researchers and others involved in the project throughout the duration of the project
n: Direct personnel expense is the salary cost of the architect, consultants, technical staff, researchers and others who work directly on the project for its duration. Overhead (indirect) costs are not tied to a single project. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, Sec. 4.3.8 (MDPE).

q: Ideal method for an architect to get his projects
n: The Code of Ethical Conduct bars self-laudatory advertising and soliciting. The proper way to get commissions is through reputation, professional association and networking. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct).

q: What do you call an architect doing post-construction services?
n: After construction, the architect may be engaged as the Building Administrator and/or Property Manager, that is, in a managerial role. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205, Sec. 10.2.

q: The owner was so happy with his architect that he decided to acquire his services after the construction of his building. What is now the role of the architect?
n: An owner who keeps the architect after construction engages him for post-construction services as Building Administrator and/or Property Manager. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205, Sec. 10.2.

q: In the context of post-construction services for an income-generating building, an architect is employed full-time by the property owner and performs daily operational tasks such as facilities oversight, tenant coordination, and maintenance supervision. Acting as a Building Administrator and/or Property Manager, which of the following most aptly describes the architect's role?
n: SPP Doc. 205 says the architect providing post-construction services works as Consulting Architect for post-construction services. That role is either dual (with being Architect-of-Record) or alone, including when acting as Building Administrator/Property Manager. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205, Sec. 10.1.

q: Under R.A. No. 9266, who is the owner of the plans and is directly and professionally responsible for the total design of the project and shall assume the civil liability for the plans, specifications and contract documents he/she has signed and sealed.
n: The Architect-of-Record owns the plans, is directly and professionally responsible for the total design, and assumes civil liability for the documents he or she signed and sealed. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 (definition of Architect-of-Record) and Sec. 20.

q: A client asks the project architect who will legally assume civil liability for the signed and sealed plans, specifications, and contract documents submitted for building permit application. The architect explains that the professional responsible must be a registered and licensed architect under R.A. 9266 who is directly and professionally accountable for the total design of the project and who signs and seals the documents. Who is this?
n: The registered architect who is directly and professionally accountable for the total design and who signs and seals the permit documents is the Architect-of-Record. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 and Sec. 20(5).

q: When an Architect-of-Record signs and seals architectural plans, specifications, architectural permits, and related contract documents, he/she legally assumes civil liability under Article 1723 of the Civil Code. For how long does this mandated civil liability last?
n: RA 9266 Sec. 20(5) says the architect who signs and seals the documents assumes the civil liability under Art. 1723 of the Civil Code for 15 years. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 20(5); Civil Code, Art. 1723.

q: What is the consequence if the Architect-of-Record (AOR) or principal architect fails to properly supervise and oversee the work of his or her staff?
o: The architect may be liable only for portions of the work that he or she personally prepared, while staff members assume responsibility for documents they produced.

The architect may remain professionally and civilly liable for errors, omissions, or deficiencies appearing in documents signed and sealed under his or her authority, even if portions were prepared by staff members.
Responsibility shifts primarily to the employee who prepared the erroneous work, provided that the architect did not participate directly in its preparation.
The architect may be relieved of liability if the work was delegated to qualified employees and reviewed by a senior project architect prior to submission.
n: The AOR answers for every document signed and sealed under his or her authority, even if staff prepared parts of it. Delegating the work does not shift the professional and civil liability. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 20(5); 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct).

q: During construction, the owner asks which architectural professional is legally responsible for the day-to-day supervision of the project, ensuring that the work conforms to the plans and specifications, monitoring the contractor's activities, and reporting deviations to the Architect-of-Record. The architect explains that this role must be performed by a registered and licensed architect under R.A. 9266. Who is this?
n: The Architect-in-Charge of Construction is the RLA who directly and professionally supervises the work on site. He or she checks that the work conforms to the plans and specifications and reports deviations. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 (definition of AICC).

q: Professionally and academically qualified and with exceptional or recognized expertise or specialization in any branch of architecture
n: A Consulting Architect is an RLA who is professionally and academically qualified and has exceptional or recognized expertise or specialization in any branch of architecture. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 (definition of Consulting Architect).

q: A real estate developer hires an architect solely for the purpose of providing high-level technical evaluation of recurring facade leaks across multiple existing buildings. The architect is engaged specifically for his expertise and specialization in building envelope diagnostic. He is tasked to review documents, analyze failures, recommend corrective strategies. and advise on long-term maintenance policies. Under R.A. 9266, which architectural role best fils this engagement? "JP
n: An architect engaged only for specialist expertise (here, diagnosing building envelopes), to review, analyze and advise, is a Consulting Architect, not the AOR or AICC. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 (definition of Consulting Architect).

q: Under the ASEAN Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA) on Architectural Services, an ASEAN architect working on a project in the Philippines must collaborate with a PRC-licensed Architect-of-Record. The ASEAN architect may provide design input but cannot sign, seal, or assume civil liability for the project. What is this professional formally called under Philippine practice?
n: A foreign architect allowed to work on a Philippine project under the ASEAN MRA collaborates with a local RLA. The foreign architect cannot sign or seal documents or assume the civil liability that RA 9266 places on the local AOR. Source: ASEAN MRA on Architectural Services (2007); RA 9266, Sec. 37 and IRR.

q: Why do some clients engage foreign architects for major or highly specialized projects?
o: To satisfy the requirements or preferences of foreign investors, operators, or multinational project stakeholders who are already familiar with the firm.
To gain access to specialized expertise, cutting-edge technologies, and innovative design methodologies developed through experience in similar projects.
To obtain a design perspective that incorporates architectural trends, cultural influences, and planning approaches from different regions of the world.
To enhance the prestige and marketability of the development through association with an internationally recognized architectural firm.
n: RA 9266 lets a foreign architect practice in the Philippines only on projects where his or her specialized expertise is needed and not available locally. Specialized expertise is therefore the reason recognized by law. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 37 and IRR.

q: A client intends to engage a foreign architect for a major development, citing the architect's international reputation and extensive project experience abroad. As a Philippine Registered and Licensed Architect, which argument would be the MOST persuasive reason to retain a local architect instead?
o: A local architect can provide a design solution that is more uniquely Filipino and culturally responsive than one prepared by a foreign architect.
A local architect generally offers a more cost-efficient professional service because there is no need to engage foreign consultants or specialists.

A local architect possesses direct knowledge of Philippine laws, permitting procedures, construction practices, and implementation requirements, allowing the project to be translated more effectively from concept to completion.
A local architect is more accessible throughout the project and can respond more quickly to issues arising during design development and construction.
n: The strongest argument is practical and legal. A local RLA knows Philippine laws, permits and construction practice and can carry the design through to completion. A foreign architect cannot sign and seal the documents anyway. Source: RA 9266, Secs. 20 and 37.

q: For which type of project would a local architect generally be most preferred?
n: Heritage sites call for familiarity with local history, culture, traditional materials and the heritage law (RA 10066), which favors a local architect. Source: RA 10066 (National Cultural Heritage Act of 2009).

q: What does AICC stand for?
n: AICC stands for Architect-in-Charge of Construction, the RLA who directly supervises construction work. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3.

q: In the context of architectural services under RA 9266, what does AOR stand for?
n: AOR stands for Architect-of-Record, the RLA who signs and seals the design documents. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3.

q: A group of professionals in architecture and allied professions, incorporated with architects for the purpose of delivering professional architectural and allied services
n: The RA 9266 IRR defines an Architectural Corporation as a group of professionals in architecture and allied professions incorporated with architects to deliver professional architectural and allied services. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 (definitions).

q: A group of two or more architects or architectural firms working in joint venture on a project basis.
n: An Association is a group of two or more architects or architectural firms in a joint venture on a project basis. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 (definitions).

q: An architectural firm, company, partnership, corporation or association may be registered and licensed provided that it is owned by at least how many percent by Registered and Licensed Architects?
n: An architectural firm, company, partnership, corporation or association may register only if Registered and Licensed Architects own at least 75% of it. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 37 and IRR.

q: A group of Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) forms a juridical entity registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The IRR of R.A. 9266 describes this entity as being synonymous with an Architectural Partnership registered with the SEC, even though the term used does not explicitly refer to a partnership or corporation. Which type of architectural juridical entity is being described?
n: The RA 9266 IRR defines an Architectural Company as synonymous with an architectural partnership registered with the SEC. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 (definitions).

q: A group of professionals composed of architects together with allied professionals forms a juridical entity for the purpose of delivering professional services in architecture and allied professions. The IRR of R.A. 9266 states that this entity must maintain at least a 75% composition of architects; otherwise, it must re-register with the SEC and the BOA to comply. Which type of juridical entity is being described?
n: An Architectural Corporation joins architects with allied professionals. Architects must make up at least 75% of it, or it must re-register with the SEC and the Board. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 37 and IRR, Sec. 3.

q: It refers to a coalition of purely Filipino professional consultants or consulting firm/s, or Filipino professional consultants or consulting firm/s in collaboration with foreign professional consultant/s and/or foreign consulting firm/s authorized to render consulting/consultancy services.
n: SPP Doc. 209 defines a Consortium or Association as a coalition of purely Filipino consultants or firms, or Filipino consultants/firms in collaboration with foreign consultants/firms authorized to render consulting services. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 209, Sec. 19.2.

q: It refers to a Filipino citizen, a natural person who possesses the qualifications of a Consultant, must be a Philippine-registered and licensed architect (RLA), must be a member in good standing of the IAPOA, and must also be an RLA specializing in any or several branch/es of the State-regulated profession of architecture as defined under R.A. No. 9266 and its derivative regulations.
n: The FPCA is a Filipino citizen and natural person with a consultant's qualifications: a Philippine RLA, a member in good standing of the IAPOA, specializing in one or more branches of architecture. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 209, Sec. 14.1.1.1.

q: Two architectural firms agree to collaborate on a single project without forming a new juridical entity. They pool expertise, share responsibilities, and operate as a formal grouping only for that specific project. Under the terminology used in architectural practice, what is this arrangement called?
n: An Association is two or more architects or firms in a joint venture on a project basis, without forming a new juridical entity. Source: RA 9266 IRR, Sec. 3 (definitions).

q: It refers to any person. whether natural or juridical, duly licensed, registered and/or duly accredited by the Commission. This also refers to a person, whether natural or juridical, duly certified/recognized by the concerned APO under the PPC or CBNE as one who possesses the appropriate knowledge and, skills, training, and relevant experience i.e. specialization/s required to perform and/or render the service/s required; must be a Philippine-registered and licensed Architect (RLA). with a valid registration certification and Commission identification (LD) card and must be a member in good standing of the [APoA
n: A Professional Consulting Architect (consultant) is any natural or juridical person, licensed or accredited by the Commission or certified by the APO, with the knowledge, skills and experience (specialization) the service requires. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 209 (definitions).

q: A major rail infrastructure project in Luzon required integrated architectural, structural, and systems engineering expertise. Three firms collaborated specifically for the MRT-7 project, pooling technical resources while retaining their separate legal identities. They did not form a new juridical entity, did not merge equity, and their collaboration existed only for that project. What is this arrangement called?
n: Separate firms that pool resources for one project but keep their own legal identities, without a new juridical entity or merged equity, form a consortium. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 209, Sec. 19.2.

q: A large Philippine architectural firm with an active design-build contracting arm teams up with another design studio, which also operates a fit-out and construction division, to jointly bid for a ₱12-billion government center annex complex. Both firms hold valid PCAB licenses for their respective design-build operations. However, the procuring agency requires them to submit one unified bid as a single contracting entity. Under RA 4566, which is enforced by the Philippine Contractors Accreditation Board (PCAB), what must the two firms secure before they can legally submit this joint bid?
o: Special Contractor's License for Multi-Disciplinary Design-Build Projects
n: PCAB rules require contractors bidding jointly as one contracting entity to secure a Joint Venture License, even if each firm already holds its own license. Source: RA 4566 (Contractors' License Law) and PCAB Implementing Rules (Joint Venture Licensing).

q: It refers to an architectural corporation. association, group or partnership duly registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) or other concerned government regulatory agency or instrumentality or to a single proprietorship duly registered with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), and likewise registered with the Commission/ Board to perform State-regulated architectural services such as professional architectural consulting services (PACS)
n: A Consulting Architectural Firm is a corporation, association, group or partnership registered with the SEC, or a sole proprietorship registered with the DTI, that is also registered with the Commission/Board to perform architectural services such as consulting. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 209 (definitions).

q: An individual Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA) practices independently and delivers architectural services under a business name registered with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI). The architect is also duly registered with the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) and accredited by the Board of Architecture (BOA). Under the IRR of R.A. 9266, which mode of architectural practice does this describe?
n: An individual RLA practicing under a DTI-registered business name is a sole proprietorship. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, Definition of Architectural Firm (DTI-registered sole proprietorship for individual practice).

q: When a business is owned by a single person, it is called a
n: A business owned by one person is a single (sole) proprietorship. The Revised Corporation Code (RA 11232) now also allows a One Person Corporation, which is not among the choices. Source: Civil Code; RA 11232 (Revised Corporation Code), Sec. 115.

q: It means the rendering by a Professional Consulting Architect (PCA) or by a consulting firm (i.e., a RAF) of independent advice, extension of technical assistance and services, as well as undertaking of activities, requiring appropriate knowledge, skills, training and experience, recognized competence, integrity, and/or financial and logistical capability.
n: SPP Doc. 209 defines consultancy services as a PCA or consulting firm rendering independent advice, technical assistance and services, and activities that require appropriate knowledge, skills, training, experience, competence, integrity and capability. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 209 (definitions).

q: Parking dimension for PWD
n: The 2024 amended BP 344 IRR requires an accessible parking slot to be at least 4,000 mm wide and 5,000 mm long. The extra 1,500 mm over a standard 2.50 m slot gives room for wheelchair passage. Source: Amended IRR of BP 344 (2024), Appendix A, Item 6.7(a).
